lessons.title: What is an Excel table?
lessons.html:
The Excel basics course showed you cells, simple formulas, AutoSum (SUM), and how to save. This course adds three next steps: tables, charts, and a few more functions.

Microsoft says that to make managing and analyzing a group of related data easier, you can turn a range of cells into an Excel table (once also called an Excel list). Do not confuse this with the separate “data tables” used for what-if analysis. This course uses the everyday table you create from a list.

A table can include:

  • A header row. By default a table has one. Each column header has filtering turned on so you can filter or sort quickly.
  • Banded rows (alternate shading) to help you see the lines.
  • A total row you can add later, with a drop-down list of functions such as SUM and AVERAGE.
  • A sizing handle in the lower-right corner so you can drag the table larger.

You can create more than one table on a sheet. Use a clear header row, such as Item, Quantity, and Amount, and sample numbers only.

This is not tax or bookkeeping advice. Keep real payroll or client files out of class practise.

lessons.title: Create a table
lessons.html:
First type a small list with a header row, the way you already can from Excel basics. Then turn that list into a table.

Microsoft’s steps to create a table quickly:

  1. Select the cell or the range that holds your data.
  2. Select Home > Format as Table.
  3. Pick a table style.
  4. In the Format as Table dialog box, select the checkbox My table as headers if you want the first row to be the header row, then click OK.

After you click OK, Excel formats the range as a table. You should see header arrows and, usually, banded rows.

If your first row is labels such as Item and Amount, keep My table as headers selected so those words stay labels, not data. If you forget, the first row of numbers may be treated as a header.

Practise with sample rows only — for example, a pretend list of hall-rental supplies. Do not use another person’s private spreadsheet.

If you cannot find Format as Table, look on the Home tab. Some versions also let you create a table from the Insert tab; this lesson follows Microsoft’s Home > Format as Table steps.

You do not need SharePoint, structured reference names, or data validation for this course.

lessons.title: Sort, filter, and a total row
lessons.html:
Once your list is a table, you can work with it faster.

Microsoft says every table column has filtering enabled in the header row so you can filter or sort quickly. Click the small arrow on a header.

  • Sort changes the order, such as A to Z or smallest to largest.
  • Filter hides rows that do not match what you chose, such as showing only one item name.

The hidden rows are still in the file. Clearing the filter brings them back. Try this on sample data so you can see the difference.

You can also add a total row. Microsoft says that once you add a total row, Excel gives you an AutoSum drop-down list with functions such as SUM and AVERAGE. When you pick one, the table converts it to a SUBTOTAL function that, by default, ignores rows hidden by a filter.

You already used SUM in Excel basics. Here, the useful new idea is that the total row can show an average as well as a sum, and that a filtered table’s total can ignore hidden rows.

You do not need to write the SUBTOTAL formula by hand for this lesson. Use the drop-down on the total row.

If you resize the table, Microsoft describes a sizing handle in the lower-right corner.

lessons.title: Make a chart from your data
lessons.html:
Microsoft says charts help you visualize data in a way that can have a clear impact. A chart turns numbers into a picture, such as columns or slices, so a group can see a pattern faster than by reading every cell.

To create a chart (Microsoft’s Windows steps):

  1. Select the data for the chart, including the header labels if you have them.
  2. Select Insert > Recommended Charts.
  3. Select a chart on the Recommended Charts tab to preview it.
  4. If you do not see one you like, select the All Charts tab to see more types.
  5. Select a chart, then select OK.

Microsoft notes that you can also select data and press Alt+F1 to create a chart right away, but it might not be the best type for your data. Recommended Charts is the safer first choice.

Keep the chart simple. One small table of sample categories and amounts is enough. After the chart appears, you can click it and add a title if your version shows that option. You do not need trendlines, 3-D pie effects, or advanced formatting for this course.

If the numbers in the table change, many charts update when the selected data changes. Check that you selected the right cells before you insert the chart.

This lesson is not a statistics class and not financial advice.

lessons.title: AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, and COUNT
lessons.html:
You already know that a formula starts with = and that SUM adds numbers. These four functions answer other everyday questions.

AVERAGE returns the average (the arithmetic mean) of its arguments. Microsoft’s example: if A1:A20 contains numbers, =AVERAGE(A1:A20) returns the average of those numbers. You can also use a shorter range, such as =AVERAGE(B2:B6).

MIN returns the smallest number in a set of values. Example: =MIN(B2:B6).

MAX returns the largest value in a set of values. Example: =MAX(B2:B6).

COUNT counts how many cells contain numbers. Microsoft’s example: =COUNT(A1:A20). Empty cells and most text are not counted. If you need to count text as well, Microsoft points to other functions such as COUNTA; this lesson stays with COUNT.

Type the formula in an empty cell next to or below your sample list, then press Enter. If the result looks wrong, click the cell and check the range in the formula bar.

You can use the same functions on a total row (Lesson 3) or by typing them yourself. Use sample volunteer hours or supply amounts — not real payroll.

This course still does not file taxes or choose a bookkeeping system.
